clinicalPearls: A rare chronic, recurrent inflammation of the choriocapillaris, retinal pigment epithelium and outer retina, usually bilateral though often asymmetric
Typically affects healthy middle-aged adults and presents with painless blurring, central or paracentral scotoma and metamorphopsia
Active lesions are grey-white, geographic patches classically beginning around the optic disc and extending centrifugally in a serpentine (snakelike) pattern
Healed areas leave scalloped zones of chorioretinal atrophy and pigment clumping, with new activity at the advancing edges of old scars
Fluorescein angiography shows early hypofluorescence of active lesions with late staining, while healed atrophic areas show window defects
Choroidal neovascularisation is an important vision-threatening complication, particularly at the margins of atrophic scars
A tuberculosis-associated serpiginous-like choroiditis must be excluded, as it requires antituberculous therapy rather than immunosuppression alone
Management principles rely on systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression to control inflammation and protect the fovea, with anti-VEGF for secondary neovascularisation
reference.pathophysiology: Serpiginous choroiditis is a chronic, presumed autoimmune inflammatory disorder targeting the choriocapillaris and overlying retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors. Recurrent bouts of inflammation cause ischaemia and destruction of the choriocapillaris, producing geographic areas of chorioretinal atrophy that spread centrifugally from the peripapillary region. Each recurrence extends from the edge of previously healed lesions, giving the characteristic serpentine advancing border. Damage to the outer retina and pigment epithelium accounts for the scotomata, and disruption of the choriocapillaris predisposes to secondary choroidal neovascularisation. An infectious (particularly tuberculous) trigger produces a clinically similar multifocal picture in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy
Age-related macular degeneration with geographic atrophy
additionalInvestigations: Fluorescein angiography to define active (early hypofluorescent, late staining) versus healed lesions
Indocyanine green angiography to reveal the extent of choriocapillaris involvement
Fundus autofluorescence to distinguish active borders from atrophic scars and monitor progression
Optical coherence tomography to assess outer retinal integrity and detect choroidal neovascularisation
Testing for latent tuberculosis (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test) and chest imaging
Syphilis serology and other infective screening to exclude mimics
redFlags: Lesion activity threatening or approaching the fovea
New subretinal fluid, haemorrhage or exudate suggesting choroidal neovascularisation
Evidence of underlying tuberculosis requiring antimicrobial rather than purely immunosuppressive therapy
reference.prognosis: Serpiginous choroiditis is a chronic relapsing disease; vision is preserved when the fovea is spared, but foveal involvement or secondary choroidal neovascularisation can cause permanent central visual loss, and recurrences may continue over many years.
pitfalls: Treating with immunosuppression without excluding tuberculosis-associated disease
Mistaking healed atrophic scarring for active inflammation, or vice versa
Missing early choroidal neovascularisation arising at the edge of an old scar
Undertreating peripapillary activity that then extends unexpectedly toward the fovea
Confusing the appearance with geographic atrophy of age-related macular degeneration in older patients
management: Suppress inflammation with systemic corticosteroids for acute flares, adding steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as antimetabolites (mycophenolate or azathioprine) or an alkylating agent for chronic control
Use adjunctive periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid to gain rapid local control of active lesions
Exclude and, where present, treat tuberculous serpiginous-like choroiditis with antituberculous therapy under corticosteroid cover before committing to immunosuppression
Treat secondary choroidal neovascularisation with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
Undertake surveillance with fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography, and angiography to detect advancing lesion edges and neovascular complications
Refer to a uveitis or ophthalmology specialist and monitor for immunosuppression-related toxicity
Provide low-vision support where foveal involvement causes permanent central visual loss
